# dsh-build-tools
Shared build tooling for DeepSeek Harness (dsh) plugins. One package replaces the copy-pasted `build
.mjs` that every `dsh-*` plugin carries, so the dual-face packaging contract lives in exactly one pl
` that every `dsh-*` plugin carries, so the dual-face packaging contract lives in exactly one place.
## The problem space
A dsh plugin is **one npm package that has to serve two very different runtimes**:
- the **host face** runs in node inside the harness. It is a Cordis plugin (`apply` / class + `injec
t`), it may open `ctx.webServer` routes, and it imports harness packages that the profile resolves a

t runtime.
- the **client face** runs in the browser. It is not loaded as a module by a bundler or a
n import map — the harness web client installs a `window.__ModuleLoader__` global, and each plugin s
cript registers itself into it as a **closure factory**: `window.__ModuleLoader__.load({ id, factory
})`. Inside that factory, `require()` resolves only against the host's frozen module table (React,
cordis, the `dsh-client-*` UI packages). Everything else must be inlined into the bundle.
So the same source tree has to produce two artifacts with two module systems, two targets, and two d
ifferent external-resolution rules — and the client one has to be wrapped in that exact registration
call or it never enters `__DSH_BOOT__` (often silently).
That wrapper is **not a hack invented by these plugins**. It mirrors what the harness does to its ow
n in-tree client packages: `packages/client/tsdown.client.ts` emits the same registration banner, th
e same `var module = { exports: {} }` intro, and the same `return module.exports; } });` footer. Out
-of-tree plugins reproduce that contract by hand, because there is no supported way to ask the harne
reproduce that contract by hand, because there is no supported way to ask the harness to bundle you.
Reproducing it by hand in every repo is the actual problem: the banner/footer strings, the platform
externals list, the host/client target split, and the extra standalone bundles for unit tests were c
opy-pasted across seven plugins. One contract change means seven manual patches, and any one of them
can drift silently.
**This package is the consolidation.** It encodes that contract once, behind options, and proves equ
ivalence with a byte-diff gate instead of eyeballing.
## What it builds
| Artifact | Format | Role |
| `lib/index.js` | ESM, node, `es2024` | host half (Cordis plugin); `@deepseek-ai/*` stays external

|
| `lib/client.js` | CJS, browser, `es2022` | client half; wrapped in the `__ModuleLoader__` regist

ration |
| `lib/<name>.mjs` | ESM, node | optional standalone modules, built without harness externa

on |
| `lib/<name>.mjs` | ESM, node | optional standalone modules, built without harness externals |
The third row is what makes the logic testable: your store/config/tool code gets its own bundle with
no cordis in it, so `node --test` can import it directly instead of mocking the harness.

## The `prepare` script
The previous pattern across these plugins was:
[代码示例省略，未执行]
That swallows build failures and silently ships whatever stale `lib/` is committed — an esbuild vers
ion mismatch or a type error becomes a plugin that loads yesterday's code and reports healthy. The p
olicy here is the opposite: **fail loudly**. Use the plain form:
[代码示例省略，未执行]
**There is no soft fallback.** This package once shipped one (`dsh-prepare-soft`), and it was remove
d because it could never work: `node build.mjs` fails in a toolchain-less install precisely because
`dsh-build-tools` cannot be resolved, and the fallback binary was provided by that same unresolvable
package. The install then failed with `command not found` (exit 127) instead of a clear build error
— a worse failure than strict prepare, not a softer one.
If a build fails, the install fails. That is the intended behavior: a plugin that quietly loads yest
erday's `lib/` and reports healthy is worse than an install that stops.
Note that npm does not run `prepare` for packages installed **from the registry** — the published ta
rball already contains the built `lib/`. So published plugins install fine on machines without the t
oolchain. `prepare` runs on git installs and on clones; those require the toolchain.
## Testing
`dsh-build-tools/test` exports a tiny zero-dependency harness — `describe` / `it` / `assertEqual` /
`assertThrows` / `runAll` — designed to run under plain `node --test`. No jest, no vitest, no config
Throws` / `runAll` — designed to run under plain `node --test`. No jest, no vitest, no config files.
**Honest recommendation:** this harness is ~120 lines. Copying it into your repo (e.g. `scripts/test
/harness.mjs`) is the suggested default — zero coupling, and you own your test stack. The subpath im
port exists for repos that prefer pulling fixes from one upstream:
[代码示例省略，未执行]
Why not Vitest? `node --test` already provides the runner, assertions, and mocks with zero dependenc
ies, and the existing plugins use it. Vitest would add watch mode, snapshots, and coverage — real DX
wins, but a dependency and config in every repo for sugar this codebase doesn't need. If you want t
hem, the harness is the seam: swap `runAll` for your runner of choice.
